<doc title="Overview" path="guide/index.md">
# Overview

CoSky provides **configuration management** and **service discovery** for microservices. A small server sits in front of **Redis**, and applications talk only to that server. Redis is the one piece of infrastructure it needs.

## How it works

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph App["Each application"]
        STARTER["Starter or client"] --> VIEW["Local view"]
    end
    SERVER["CoSky server<br>+ Dashboard"]
    REDIS[("Redis")]
    STARTER -- "writes, leases: gRPC" --> SERVER
    SERVER -- "changes: Watch" --> VIEW
    SERVER --> REDIS
```

- **Writes** go through the server, which applies each one atomically and gives the namespace a new revision.
- **Reads** come from a view in each application's memory, so they cost no network round trip.
- **Changes** reach every view over a Watch stream. A client that was away resumes from the revision it last saw.
- **Everything is a resource**: a Config, an Instance, a Namespace, a Role. They share one API, over gRPC and REST.

[Architecture](./architecture.md) explains the data model and the consistency guarantees.

## Features

| Area | What you get |
|---|---|
| Configuration | Spring Boot `spring.config.import` with live refresh; YAML, JSON, properties and text; revisions with rollback; zip import and export |
| Service discovery | Spring Cloud `DiscoveryClient`, `ServiceRegistry` and LoadBalancer; instances under a lease; metadata and weights; fixed instances |
| Resilience | Local views keep serving through an outage; a snapshot on disk survives a restart; mass expiry protection; several server replicas |
| Security | ServiceAccount tokens and OIDC on every call, data plane included; roles scoped to namespaces and name prefixes; TLS; a structured audit log |
| Operations | One image with the Dashboard; Kustomize manifests; Prometheus metrics; OpenTelemetry traces; topology of who watches whom |

## When CoSky fits

- You already run Redis, and would rather not add a consensus system to your stack.
- A namespace holds up to about 50,000 instances and 10,000 Configs, the size [measured](./performance.md).
- You want Spring Cloud integration, or Kotlin, or can generate a gRPC or REST client from its protos and OpenAPI document.

## When it does not

- Your data must survive any single failure without loss. Redis replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose the last writes. CoSky notices and recovers, as [Architecture](./architecture.md) describes, but it cannot bring them back. Use a Raft-based system instead.
- You need health checks run by the server. Instances stay alive by renewing a lease, and CoSky does not probe them.
- You need a client for another language off the shelf. Only Kotlin has one; other languages use the protos.

## Where to go next

| Goal | Page |
|---|---|
| Run it in five minutes | [Getting Started](./getting-started.md) |
| Serve Spring properties | [Configuration](./configuration.md) |
| Register and find services | [Service Discovery](./service-discovery.md) |
| Use it without Spring | [Using the SDK](./sdk.md) |
| Run it in production | [Deployment](./deployment.md), [Security](./security.md) |
| Move from CoSky 6.x | [Moving from 6.x](./upgrade-8.md) |
| Look up a property or an endpoint | [Configuration Properties](./properties.md), [REST API](./rest-api.md) |
</doc>

<doc title="Getting Started" path="guide/getting-started.md">
# Getting Started

::: warning 8.0 is in alpha
`8.0.0-alpha.2` is a preview with no compatibility promise: its API, wire format and Redis keys may still change. `ahoowang/cosky:latest` is still 6.x, whose documentation is in the [`v6` branch](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/tree/v6/wiki/guide).
:::

This takes a server in development mode and a Spring Boot 4 application. [Requirements](./requirements.md) lists the versions.

## 1. Start a server

```bash
docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 9090:9090 ahoowang/cosky:8.0.0-alpha.2 --dev
```

`--dev` needs no Redis and no sign-in. Nothing survives a restart, so never run it for real: [Deployment](./deployment.md) shows how. Port 9090 serves applications over gRPC. Port 8080 serves the REST API and the Dashboard, at <http://localhost:8080>.

## 2. Add the starter

```kotlin
dependencies {
    implementation(platform("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:4.1.0"))
    implementation(platform("org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-dependencies:2025.1.2"))
    implementation(platform("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-bom:8.0.0-alpha.2"))
    implementation("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-spring-boot-starter")
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webflux")
    implementation("org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-context") // for live refresh
}
```

In Kotlin, add the `kotlin("plugin.spring")` Gradle plugin as well: the bean in `@RefreshScope` below has to be open.

## 3. Configure the application

```yaml
# application.yaml
server:
  port: 8081 # 8080 is the CoSky server
spring:
  application:
    name: provider
  config:
    import: "optional:cosky:provider.yaml"
  cloud:
    # Spring Cloud 2025.1 declares Spring Boot 4.0. Remove this once on Spring Cloud 2026.0.
    compatibility-verifier:
      enabled: false
cosky:
  endpoints: localhost:9090
  namespace: default
```

The application registers itself as the service `provider` once its web server is up, and imports the Config `provider.yaml`. `optional:` lets it start while that Config does not exist yet.

## 4. Create a Config

```bash
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/default/configs/provider.yaml \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"config":{"format":"CONFIG_FORMAT_YAML","content":"example:\n  greeting: Bonjour"}}'
```

A bean in `@RefreshScope` sees the new value without a restart:

```kotlin
@RestController
@RefreshScope
class HelloController(@Value("\${example.greeting:Hello}") private val greeting: String) {
    @GetMapping("/hello/{name}", produces = [MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE])
    fun hello(@PathVariable name: String): String = "$greeting, $name"
}
```

## 5. Find it from another application

Add `spring-cloud-starter-loadbalancer` to a second application with the same settings and its own name and port, and call the provider by its service name:

```kotlin
@Bean
@LoadBalanced
fun webClientBuilder(): WebClient.Builder = WebClient.builder()

// ...
builder.baseUrl("http://provider").build().get().uri("/hello/World").retrieve().awaitBody<String>()
```

## 6. Look around

Open the [Dashboard](./dashboard.md) at <http://localhost:8080>. Instances show up under **Service**, with **Leased** next to them, and the topology on the first page shows who calls whom.

```bash
curl localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/default/views/topology
```

## See it run

The repository holds this as a working example. `examples/README.md` walks through it:

```bash
./gradlew :server:run --args='--dev'
```

```bash
./gradlew :examples:provider:run
```

```bash
./gradlew :examples:consumer:run
```

## Next steps

- [Configuration](./configuration.md): formats, revisions, rollback and import.
- [Service Discovery](./service-discovery.md): leases, weights and fixed instances.
- [Deployment](./deployment.md) and [Security](./security.md): before real traffic.
</doc>

<doc title="Configuration" path="guide/configuration.md">
# Configuration

A **Config** is a named document in a namespace: a name, a format and its content, up to 1 MiB.

| Field | Rules |
|---|---|
| Name | Letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-` and `/`, up to 253 characters. `shared/datasource.yaml` is one name. |
| Format | `YAML`, `JSON`, `PROPERTIES` or `TEXT`, declared with the Config. Only importing a zip file guesses it, from the file extension. |
| Content | UTF-8. The server keeps its SHA-256, which you can compare and cannot set. |

## Loading into Spring

```yaml
spring:
  config:
    import: "optional:cosky:order-service.yaml,cosky:shared/datasource.yaml"
cosky:
  endpoints: cosky.internal:9090
  token: ${COSKY_TOKEN}
  namespace: prod
```

- Only `default` exists at first. Create any other namespace before using it: `curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod -H "Authorization: Bearer $COSKY_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"namespace":{}}'`.
- `cosky:` without `optional:` fails the start when the Config cannot be loaded, including when no server can be reached and no snapshot holds it. When the server refuses, the start fails at once, and the log says why.
- YAML and JSON are parsed as YAML, and properties as properties. A TEXT Config becomes one property named after the Config.
- `cosky.config.load-timeout` (5 seconds) limits how long an import waits for the server.
- An import connects with what is known of `cosky.*` when its file is read, so keep these settings in the same file or in the environment. Spring reads `application.yaml` before `application-prod.yaml`, whose settings do not reach an import in the former.

## Live refresh

With `spring-cloud-context` on the classpath, a change to an imported Config publishes a Spring Cloud `RefreshEvent`, so beans in `@RefreshScope` and `@ConfigurationProperties` beans see it. This holds for a Config that did not exist at start as well. Turn it off with `cosky.config.refresh.enabled: false`.

The application compares against what it loaded, so a change made between loading and watching still counts.

When an `optional:` Config is deleted, its values leave the application on that refresh. A required one keeps its last values and logs a warning, because there is nothing to fall back on, and picks up again when the Config comes back. This also holds for an application starting from a [snapshot](./sdk.md#snapshots) that the server no longer agrees with: it starts with what the snapshot holds, then follows the server once connected.

## Writing

Use the [Dashboard](./dashboard.md) or the [REST API](./rest-api.md). A write replaces the whole Config:

```bash
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod/configs/shared%2Fdatasource.yaml \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $COSKY_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'If-Match: "42"' \
  -d '{"config":{"format":"CONFIG_FORMAT_YAML","content":"url: jdbc:mysql://db/orders"}}'
```

| Header | Means |
|---|---|
| `If-Match: "42"` | Only if it is still at revision 42. Otherwise `409`, and nothing changes. |
| `If-None-Match: *` | Only if it does not exist. |
| Neither | Write regardless. |

The Dashboard always sends the first two, so nobody overwrites a change they did not see. Writing the same content changes nothing: there is no new revision and no event.

A `/` in a name is encoded as `%2F` in the path, because a name is one path segment.

## History and rollback

Each Config keeps its last 20 revisions, newest first:

```bash
curl localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod/configs/app.yaml/history
```

Rolling back writes the content of an earlier revision as a new one, so the history only grows:

```bash
curl -X POST localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod/configs/app.yaml:rollback \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"toRevision":"41"}'
```

A deleted Config keeps its history until it is created again or its namespace is deleted, and a rollback brings it back.

## Import and export

A zip file moves many Configs at once. Each entry path is a Config name, and its extension decides the format.

```bash
curl -o configs.zip localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod/configs:export
```

```bash
curl -X POST localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/staging/configs:import --data-binary @configs.zip
```

An import overwrites Configs of the same name, and holds at most 10,000 entries.

## Keeping secrets

Config content is not encrypted, on the server or in the [snapshots](./sdk.md#snapshots) clients keep on disk. Turn snapshots of Configs off with `cosky.snapshot.include-config: false`, and keep real secrets in a system made for them.
</doc>

<doc title="Service Discovery" path="guide/service-discovery.md">
# Service Discovery

An **Instance** is one running copy of a service: a service name, an endpoint, a weight and metadata. A service is simply the group of Instances that share a name.

## Registering

With the starter, an application registers once its web server is ready, and removes itself on shutdown.

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
cosky:
  registry:
    enabled: true
    weight: 1
    metadata:
      zone: az1
```

- The service is `spring.application.name`, which must be a DNS-style name: lowercase letters, digits, `-` and `.`, up to 63 characters. `OrderService` is refused.
- A separate management port is not registered.
- `spring.cloud.service-registry.auto-registration.enabled: false` turns registering off.

## Leases

A process holds one lease per namespace, however many instances it registers, and renews it every third of its TTL (30 seconds by default). When renewals stop, its instances go.

| Event | What happens |
|---|---|
| Clean shutdown | The lease is revoked within 3 seconds, and the instances go at once. |
| Crash | The lease expires, and the instances go a third of the TTL later: 40 seconds by default. |
| Lease lost, such as after a Redis failover | The client notices, waits up to 5 seconds so that not everyone returns at once, and registers everything again. |
| Client reconnects | It renews at once, without waiting for the next period. |

Allowed TTLs are 5 to 300 seconds.

## Finding services

`DiscoveryClient` and `ReactiveDiscoveryClient` read the local view. The first read of a service waits up to `cosky.discovery.load-timeout` (5 seconds), so that "not known yet" is not mistaken for "empty". If the server refuses, for lack of permission or because the namespace does not exist, the read throws a `CoSkyException` at once. Afterwards, a read costs no network round trip.

Add `spring-cloud-starter-loadbalancer`, and `@LoadBalanced` clients get their instances from CoSky, with Spring Cloud's own algorithms choosing among them.

## Weights

A weight of `0` keeps an instance registered but takes it out of rotation, which is how to drain one: load balancers leave it out, while `DiscoveryClient` still lists it. The Kotlin client's load balancer picks at random in proportion to weight. Spring Cloud LoadBalancer's default round robin treats every other weight alike.

An operator can set it on an instance an application registered. It lasts until the application registers again, after restarting or losing its lease.

## Fixed instances

An Instance without a lease stays until someone deletes it. Use this for something that cannot register itself, such as a database:

```bash
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/namespaces/prod/instances/orders-db \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"instance":{"service":"orders-db","endpoint":{"scheme":"tcp","host":"10.0.0.5","port":3306}}}'
```

The Dashboard marks each instance **Leased** or **Fixed**. Nothing checks whether a fixed instance is alive.

## Moving an instance to another service

An instance stays in the service it was created in. A write with another service is refused with `INVALID_ARGUMENT` (HTTP 400): delete the instance, then create it again. The default instance name holds the service, so this only comes up with a name of your own. An application registering under such a name for a new service is refused until the old registration is gone, which takes at most its lease's TTL if the old process did not stop cleanly.

## When things fail

CoSky favours keeping a stale instance over dropping a live one, and callers are expected to retry and use circuit breakers.

| Failure | What applications see |
|---|---|
| Server unreachable | Reads keep serving the last view, and the health indicator stays `UP` with `connection: DEGRADED`, because a restart would not help. |
| Restart while the server is away | The view comes back from the [snapshot](./sdk.md#snapshots) on disk. |
| Server or network was down for longer than the TTL | The reaper waits 30 seconds after recovering, so that live clients can renew rather than be removed. |
| More than half of a namespace's leases expire at once | Reaping pauses, as this looks like a partition. It resumes when the share falls, or after 5 minutes regardless. |
| Redis fails over and loses recent writes | Every replica notices the revision going backwards, and clients start over from a fresh snapshot. Writes that were lost stay lost. |

These all have settings under [`cosky.lease`](./properties.md#server). A process that really crashed during such a pause stays listed for up to 5 minutes longer.

## Who calls whom

A client that watches a service counts as consuming it. The topology on the [Dashboard](./dashboard.md) and at `/views/topology` shows these edges, under the name in `spring.application.name`, or the signed-in subject without one. They expire 90 seconds after the last replica saw the watch, so a stopped consumer disappears by itself.
</doc>

<doc title="Using the SDK" path="guide/sdk.md">
# Using the SDK

`cosky-client` is a coroutine client with no dependency on Spring or Redis. The starter is built on it. It needs JDK 21 or later.

```kotlin
implementation("me.ahoo.cosky:cosky-client:8.0.0-alpha.2")
```

```kotlin
val client = CoSkyClient(
    CoSkyClientOptions(
        endpoints = listOf("cosky-0.internal:9090", "cosky-1.internal:9090"),
        token = System.getenv("COSKY_TOKEN"),
        clientName = "order-service",
    ),
)
val prod = client.namespace("prod")
```

## Reading Configs

```kotlin
// Once, waiting for the first view.
val config: Resource? = prod.configs.load("order-service.yaml")

// Always current, from memory.
val current: StateFlow<Resource?> = prod.configs.watch("order-service.yaml")
current.collect { apply(it?.config?.content) }
```

`load` throws a `CoSkyException` when the server refuses the watch, such as for lack of permission or because the namespace does not exist, unless a snapshot knows better. The watch keeps trying, so a later `load` works once that changes.

## Finding instances

```kotlin
val instances: StateFlow<List<Resource>> = prod.instances.watch("payment")
val services: Set<String> = prod.instances.services()

val balancer = prod.loadBalancer("payment")
val chosen: Resource? = balancer.choose()
```

`choose()` picks at random in proportion to weight, allocates nothing and does not suspend. It returns `null` when no instance can be chosen.

## Registering

```kotlin
val registration = prod.instances.register(
    service = "order-service",
    endpoint = endpoint {
        scheme = "http"
        host = "10.0.0.7"
        port = 8080
    },
    metadata = mapOf("zone" to "az1"),
    weight = 2,
)
// ...
registration.close()
```

The client keeps the lease alive, and registers everything again if the lease is lost. Closing the last registration ends the lease.

## Closing

`client.close()` revokes its leases within 3 seconds. After that the server expires them.

## Connection states

`client.connectionState` is a `StateFlow`:

| State | Means |
|---|---|
| `CONNECTING` | No server has answered yet. |
| `SYNCED` | Following a server. |
| `DEGRADED` | Not connected: serving what is known, from memory or a snapshot. |
| `CLOSED` | Closed. |

Reconnecting backs off from 100 ms to 10 seconds with jitter, moving through the endpoints in turn.

## Snapshots

The client writes its views to `~/.cosky` (`snapshotDir`, or `cosky.snapshot.dir` with the starter) and starts from them after a restart, in `DEGRADED`, until it reaches a server. This helps a process restarting on the same disk. In Kubernetes it takes a persistent volume.

Snapshots are not encrypted. The directory is `0700` and the files `0600`. `snapshotIncludeConfig = false` keeps Config contents off the disk, and `snapshotDir = null` turns snapshots off.

## TLS

```kotlin
CoSkyClientOptions(
    endpoints = listOf("cosky.internal:9090"),
    tls = true,
    tlsTrustedCertificates = Path.of("/etc/cosky/ca.pem"), // for a private CA
)
```

See [Security](./security.md#tls). For anything else, `channelFactory` builds the gRPC channel yourself.

## Writing

The client reads, registers and renews. To manage resources from code, use the generated gRPC stubs in `cosky-api`:

```kotlin
val resources = ResourceServiceGrpcKt.ResourceServiceCoroutineStub(channel)
resources.put(putRequest { resource = /* ... */ })
```

## Java

`cosky-client` exposes coroutines, which are awkward from Java. A Java facade is planned for 8.1. Until then, Java applications use the Spring Boot starter, which needs no Kotlin in your code.

## Other languages

Nothing in the client is privileged: everything goes through the public protocol. The protos are in `api/src/main/proto`, and `./gradlew :api:generateOpenApi` writes the OpenAPI document to `api/build/openapi/cosky.yaml`. A conforming client has to follow what the [design](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/docs/architecture-redesign.md) says about Watch positions and lease renewal, and `conformance-test` holds the suite the Kotlin client passes.
</doc>

<doc title="Deployment" path="guide/deployment.md">
# Deployment

The server is one image, `ahoowang/cosky` (also `ghcr.io/ahoo-wang/cosky`), holding the Dashboard too. Run at least two replicas: they share nothing but Redis, and clients move between them by themselves.

| Port | Serves |
|---|---|
| `8080` | REST API, Dashboard, Actuator |
| `9090` | gRPC, for applications |

## Redis

CoSky needs **Redis 7.0 or later, or Valkey 8**, with `maxmemory-policy noeviction`. The server checks both at start and refuses to run otherwise, because an eviction would silently lose objects and Watch history. It works on a single node, Sentinel or a Cluster, and each namespace stays in one slot.

Redis replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose the last writes. To narrow that window, set `min-replicas-to-write 1` on the primary. CoSky notices a lost timeline and recovers, as [Architecture](./architecture.md#when-redis-loses-writes) explains, and clients register again. A Config written just before the failover may be gone.

If Redis loses everything, the server sets it up again by itself within about 30 seconds, as on a first start: the system namespace, `default`, and the admin from the bootstrap token, so leave that token set. The rest is gone: other namespaces, Configs, Roles, RoleBindings, and ServiceAccounts with their tokens. Create them again, or import a [zip export](./configuration.md#import-and-export) of your Configs. With auth on, applications keep serving what they know and stay unregistered until they have a new token. With auth off, they follow what is there once their namespace exists, and register themselves.

## Docker

```bash
docker network create cosky
```

```bash
docker run -d --name redis --network cosky redis:7.4
```

```bash
export COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN="cosky_$(openssl rand -hex 8)_$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
echo "$COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN"
```

```bash
docker run -d --name cosky --network cosky -p 8080:8080 -p 9090:9090 \
  -e COSKY_STORE_REDIS_URI=redis://redis:6379 \
  -e COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN \
  ahoowang/cosky:8.0.0-alpha.2
```

Keep that token: it is the admin of a new installation, as [Security](./security.md#the-first-token) explains. For a Redis Cluster, add `-e COSKY_STORE_REDIS_CLUSTER=true`.

Any [property](./properties.md) can be set as an environment variable or an argument. `--dev` runs in memory without sign-in, for trying things out only.

## Kubernetes

The repository holds [Kustomize](https://kustomize.io) manifests: a Deployment of three replicas, a Service and a PodDisruptionBudget.

```bash
kubectl create secret generic cosky-redis --from-literal=uri=redis://redis:6379
```

```bash
kubectl create secret generic cosky-auth --from-literal=bootstrap-token="cosky_$(openssl rand -hex 8)_$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
```

```bash
kubectl apply -k k8s/base
```

For a Redis Cluster, apply `k8s/overlays/redis-cluster` instead. Your own overlay of a few lines can set the namespace, the image tag or the resources: that one shows the shape.

Probes use `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`. A replica reports ready once it has loaded the namespaces, which for 50,000 instances and 10,000 Configs [took 2 to 3.5 seconds](./performance.md).

A replica stays ready while Redis is away, on purpose. Redis is shared, so a failover would otherwise take every replica out of the Service at once, while they can still serve what they know. The cost is that a replica cut off from Redis on its own goes on serving what it last knew. Replicas that disagree on `cosky_cache_revision{namespace}` for more than a minute show this, and restarting that one ends it.

## Rolling updates

In Kubernetes a stopping replica first waits 5 seconds, for the Service to stop sending it connections. Then it ends its streams, after up to 5 seconds, and clients reconnect to another one and resume where they were. If they fell out of the Watch window meanwhile, they read a fresh snapshot, which costs a little more and loses nothing. `cosky_watch_gone_total` shows whether this happens, and `cosky.watch.window` is the setting to raise if it does, along with `cosky.watch.window-bytes` if your Configs are large.

## The Dashboard on its own

The image serves the Dashboard at `/`. To host it elsewhere, put it behind a reverse proxy that also forwards `/v1` to the server: the page expects the API on its own origin, and the server has no CORS.

## Observability

Metrics are at `/actuator/prometheus`:

| Metric | Watch for |
|---|---|
| `cosky_cache_lag_seconds{namespace}` | Writes taking long to reach a replica |
| `cosky_cache_revision{namespace}` | Replicas that disagree for long: one of them is cut off from Redis |
| `cosky_store_apply_seconds` | Write latency |
| `cosky_watch_active` | Watches on this replica |
| `cosky_watch_gone_total{reason}` | Clients having to start over: `slow`, `compacted`, `epoch`, `regression` |
| `cosky_lease_active{namespace}`, `cosky_lease_expired_total` | Registered processes and expiries |
| `cosky_lease_protection_active{namespace}` | Reaping paused by a mass expiry |
| `cosky_revision_regression_total` | Redis lost writes |
| `cosky_anti_entropy_drift_total{namespace}` | A replica's view differed from the store, which should never happen |
| `cosky_auth_failures_total{reason}` | Failed sign-ins |

**Traces** cover gRPC and HTTP at a 10% sample. To export them, set `management.opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint`, such as `http://collector:4318/v1/traces`.

**Audit**: every write and every authentication failure is one JSON line in the log. Collect those with the rest of your logs. See [Security](./security.md#audit).

## Sizing

[Performance](./performance.md) has the measurements. As a starting point, 512 MB of heap holds a namespace of 10,000 objects with room to spare, and memory grows by about 1.5 KB per object. The image sets `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` and compact object headers, so give the container what the heap should be, plus a quarter.

Large Configs need their own thought, because what is kept for resuming includes their content:

- **A replica** keeps at most `cosky.watch.window-bytes` (64 MB) of recent changes per namespace, on top of every object. Past that, a client that fell behind reads a fresh snapshot.
- **Redis** has no such limit: it keeps the last `cosky.watch.window` changes of each namespace, and the last 20 revisions of each Config. Writing a 1 MB Config 800 times took 825 MB. Size Redis for how often your large Configs change, or lower `cosky.watch.window`. At `maxmemory`, writes fail rather than anything being evicted.
</doc>

<doc title="Security" path="guide/security.md">
# Security

Every call goes through the server and is checked there, including what applications do. Nothing but the server touches Redis, so protect Redis and its credentials as you would the data itself.

## Who is calling

| Subject | Signs in with | For |
|---|---|---|
| `SERVICE_ACCOUNT` | A token, `cosky_<id>_<secret>` | Programs, and people without OIDC |
| `USER` and `GROUP` | An OIDC ID token | People |

A token goes in `Authorization: Bearer`, over gRPC and HTTP alike. The server keeps only its SHA-256, and shows the plaintext once, when creating it.

An account holds at most two tokens, which allows rotating without a gap: create the second, move the programs over, revoke the first. Revoking takes effect at once, including on open streams.

### The first token

On its first start, a server without any role binding turns `COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` into the `admin` ServiceAccount, with the `admin` role in every namespace. Use it to create real accounts, then revoke it.

```bash
export COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN="cosky_$(openssl rand -hex 8)_$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
```

- The server reads it only while no role binding exists. After that another value does nothing, so removing it changes nothing either.
- Without it, a server with no role binding starts and logs a warning, and nobody can sign in.
- To replace a lost token, run one server on the same Redis with `--cosky.auth.enabled=false`, where nobody else can reach it. Create a token with `POST /v1/serviceaccounts/admin/tokens`, revoke the lost one, and stop that server.

### OIDC

```yaml
cosky:
  auth:
    oidc:
      issuer: https://idp.example.com/realms/main
      client-id: cosky-dashboard
```

The server checks signature, issuer, audience and expiry against the provider's keys. `sub` becomes the `USER` name, and the `groups` claim (see `groups-claim`) the `GROUP` names. The token's audience must be `audience`, or the client when that is not set.

The Dashboard signs in through the authorization code flow with PKCE, so register `cosky-dashboard` as a public client, with the Dashboard's address as its redirect URI and as the address to return to after signing out. The provider must allow that origin to call its token endpoint, and browsers and the server must reach the issuer at the same address. `GET /v1/auth/config` gives the page these public values before anyone has signed in, and holds nothing else.

`scopes` defaults to `openid` and `profile`. Add a scope only if your provider has it, because it refuses a request for one it does not know. Some providers ask for one to send groups, and some for `offline_access` to give a refresh token.

- **Staying signed in.** The Dashboard renews the ID token before it expires, using the refresh token. A provider that gives none leaves people to sign in again when the token expires, which takes 5 minutes on a default Keycloak. The refresh token stays in the tab, next to the ID token, and ends with it.
- **Signing out** also ends the session at the provider, so that the next sign-in asks for a password, if the provider has an `end_session_endpoint`.
- **When the provider is away,** servers still start, and applications carry on with their tokens. People already signed in carry on until their ID token expires, and new sign-ins fail: the server answers `UNAVAILABLE` rather than calling the token invalid. Keep a ServiceAccount token to get in meanwhile.

### Keycloak

This was tried with Keycloak 26. Other providers follow the same standard, but none has been tried.

1. Create the client `cosky-dashboard`, with client authentication off and the standard flow on. Set its valid redirect URIs to `https://cosky.example.com/*` and its web origins to `https://cosky.example.com`.
2. In the client's dedicated scope, add a **Group Membership** mapper with the token claim name `groups`, **Full group path** off, and **Add to ID token** on. With the full path on, a group's name is `/devs`.
3. Bind a role to the group. A person's `sub` is an opaque id, so groups are easier. Someone with no role yet sees their `sub` and groups in the Dashboard, to pass on to you.

```bash
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/v1/rolebindings/devs-view \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $COSKY_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"roleBinding":{"role":"viewer","subjects":[{"type":"TYPE_GROUP","name":"devs"}],"namespaces":["*"]}}'
```

## Who may do what

A **Role** holds rules, and a **RoleBinding** gives a role to subjects in some namespaces. Three roles are built in, and a Role cannot take their names:

| Role | Allows |
|---|---|
| `admin` | Everything |
| `viewer` | Reading and watching everything |
| `client` | Reading and watching Configs, and reading, watching and writing Instances |

Your own roles look like this:

```json
{
  "role": {
    "description": "Runs the order service",
    "rules": [
      {"kinds": ["KIND_INSTANCE"], "namespaces": ["*"], "verbs": ["VERB_PUT", "VERB_DELETE"], "names": ["order"]},
      {"kinds": ["KIND_INSTANCE"], "namespaces": ["*"], "verbs": ["VERB_GET", "VERB_WATCH"]},
      {"kinds": ["KIND_CONFIG"], "namespaces": ["*"], "verbs": ["VERB_GET", "VERB_WATCH"], "names": ["order-service.yaml", "shared/*"]}
    ]
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "roleBinding": {
    "role": "order-service",
    "subjects": [{"type": "TYPE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT", "name": "order"}],
    "namespaces": ["prod"]
  }
}
```

- A call is allowed when any rule of any bound role matches it. A rule applies only where its own namespaces and the binding's overlap.
- `names` left empty matches everything. Otherwise it holds exact values, or prefixes ending in `*`, matched against the Config name, the Instance's **service**, or the object name.
- Global kinds (Namespace, ServiceAccount, Role, RoleBinding) live in the namespace `_system`.
- `GET` includes lists, and only what the rule allows shows up in them.
- A lease belongs to whoever took it, so one account cannot attach its instances to another's lease.
- A change to a role reaches open Watch streams: one that lost permission is canceled.

`GET /v1/me` shows who the server thinks you are, and your effective rules.

With `cosky.auth.enabled: false` everyone may do everything. It is for development only.

## TLS

Without TLS, tokens cross the network in the clear, so turn it on in production. The server uses Spring's SSL bundles:

```yaml
spring:
  ssl:
    bundle:
      jks:
        cosky:
          keystore:
            location: file:/etc/cosky/server.p12
            password: ${KEYSTORE_PASSWORD}
            type: PKCS12
  grpc:
    server:
      ssl:
        bundle: cosky
server:
  ssl:
    bundle: cosky
```

And clients:

```yaml
cosky:
  tls:
    enabled: true
    trusted-certificates: /etc/cosky/ca.pem   # for a private CA; otherwise the JVM's trust store decides
```

Mutual TLS is not supported yet: a client proves who it is with its token.

With TLS on, port 8080 speaks only HTTPS, while the image's health check and the probes in `k8s/base` use HTTP. Give them a plain port of their own:

```yaml
management:
  server:
    port: 8081
    ssl:
      enabled: false
```

Then point the probes at it, and the container's check too: `docker run --health-cmd 'curl -f http://localhost:8081/actuator/health/liveness || exit 1'`.

## Audit

Each write and each failed sign-in is one JSON line in the log, with the time, subject, verb, kind, namespace, name, revision, outcome and remote address. Config contents and tokens never appear. The server keeps no audit data of its own: collect the lines with your log system, which also decides how long they stay.

## What is not protected

- Config contents are not encrypted, in Redis or in client [snapshots](./sdk.md#snapshots).
- Anyone who can reach Redis can read and change everything, past all of the above.
- Instance metadata is visible to anyone allowed to read the instance.
- `/actuator/health`, `/actuator/info` and `/actuator/prometheus` on port 8080 need no token, and the metrics name your namespaces. Keep them off public networks, or move them with `management.server.port`.
- gRPC health on port 9090 needs no token. gRPC reflection is off, and `spring.grpc.server.reflection.enabled` turns it on.
</doc>

<doc title="Dashboard" path="guide/dashboard.md">
# Dashboard

The server hosts the Dashboard at `/`, on port 8080. It uses only the public [REST API](./rest-api.md), so it can do nothing you could not do with `curl`, and your [roles](./security.md#who-may-do-what) apply to it. A refused action shows the server's reason.

![Dashboard](/dashboard-dashboard.png)

## Signing in

Paste a ServiceAccount token, or use the OIDC button when the server [offers one](./security.md#oidc). The token stays in that browser tab, and goes when the tab closes. A server with `cosky.auth.enabled: false` asks for nothing.

## Pages

The namespace selector in the header decides what every page shows.

| Page | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Dashboard** | Counts of services, instances, Configs and namespaces, and the topology of who watches whom |
| **Configuration** | Create, edit, delete, import and export Configs; compare any revision with the current one, and roll back |
| **Service** | Services and their instances, leased or fixed; add, edit and delete instances |
| **Namespace** | Create and delete namespaces. Only an empty one can be deleted, and not the one selected. |
| **Service Account** | Accounts and their tokens. A new token shows once, so copy it then. |
| **Role** and **Role Binding** | Who may do what, and where |

![Configuration](/dashboard-config.png)

## Staying current

The Configuration and Service pages follow changes as they happen, over a server-sent event stream, without a reload. A stream that breaks or goes silent is opened again. The first page reads its counts every 30 seconds, so that it does not hold a connection of its own: browsers allow few per server over HTTP/1.1.

## Editing safely

An edit remembers the revision it started from. If someone changed the object in the meantime, saving fails with the server's reason and changes nothing, so reload and try again.
</doc>

<doc title="Moving from 6.x" path="guide/upgrade-8.md">
# Moving from 6.x

CoSky 8.0 is a new system, and nothing from 6.x carries over by itself. Applications on 6.x talk to Redis directly, and applications on 8.0 talk to the server, so **neither generation can see the other's instances**. There is no bridge: applications move together, in one cutover.

If some services must call each other across generations during a move, run the two installations side by side and switch traffic between whole environments.

## What changes

| | 6.x | 8.0 |
|---|---|---|
| Applications reach | Redis, directly | The server, over gRPC |
| Authentication of applications | None | A token on every call |
| Starters | `cosky-spring-cloud-starter-config`, `cosky-spring-cloud-starter-discovery` | `cosky-spring-boot-starter` |
| Loading configuration | `bootstrap.yaml` | `spring.config.import` |
| Settings | `spring.cloud.cosky.*`, `spring.data.redis.*` | `cosky.*` |
| Namespaces | Any name, often `{dev}` or `cosky-{default}` | DNS labels, such as `dev` or `default` |
| Service names | Anything | DNS-style names, lowercase |
| Config formats | Guessed from the extension | Declared with the Config |
| Staying alive | Each instance's own TTL | One lease per process |
| Applications without a web server | Registered, given `registry.port` | Do not register by themselves: call the client's `instances.register` |
| Taking an instance out of rotation | `ServiceRegistry.setStatus` | A weight of `0` |
| People | Users with passwords | OIDC, or ServiceAccount tokens |
| Permissions | Read or write per namespace | Roles down to kinds, verbs and name prefixes |
| Audit | A page in the Dashboard | JSON lines in the log |
| Redis | Any version | 7.0 or later, `noeviction` |
| JDK | 17 | 21 for clients, 25 for the server |

## What moves

| | How |
|---|---|
| Configs, with their history if you like | `cosky-migrate` |
| Instances that register themselves | They do so on 8.0 when they switch |
| Fixed instances | By hand, from the report |
| Users and roles | By hand, from the report |
| Audit log and topology | They do not. The audit log stays in 6.x's Redis, and topology rebuilds itself. |

Revisions and timestamps start anew. A Config removed in 6.x has no current version, and does not arrive.

## Getting the tool

Each [release](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/releases) carries `cosky-migrate` as a zip file. Unpack it, and run `bin/cosky-migrate` with JDK 21 or later.

To build it instead, with JDK 21 installed:

```bash
./gradlew :migration:installDist
```

The tool is then at `migration/build/install/cosky-migrate/bin/cosky-migrate`.

## The cutover

**1. Start 8.0.** It may share the Redis of 6.x if that Redis meets the [requirements](./requirements.md): their keys do not overlap.

**2. Rehearse while 6.x still runs.** This reads both sides, writes nothing, and writes a report:

```bash
export COSKY_TOKEN=<bootstrap token>
cosky-migrate --source redis://6x-redis:6379 --target http://cosky:8080 --dry-run
```

Read `cosky-migration-report.md`:

- **Service names to change.** `OrderService` cannot register on 8.0, so change `spring.application.name`.
- **Namespaces 8.0 cannot name.** `cosky-{default}` goes to `default` and `{dev}` to `dev`, while anything else illegal stops the run. Name it with `--namespace 'Old_Name=new-name'`, or leave it out with `--namespace 'Old_Name='`. A namespace 6.x never listed must be named this way too.
- **Configs 8.0 refuses**, such as a name holding `:` or content over 1 MiB.

**3. Rebuild people and permissions.** The report lists every 6.x role with the 8.0 rule each grant corresponds to, and every user with their roles. Create those roles and bindings, and a ServiceAccount with a token for each application. An application without a token cannot do anything on a server with auth on.

**4. Prepare the applications.** Replace the starters, move `bootstrap.yaml` into `application.yaml`, and set the token. On Spring Boot 4.1, also set `spring.cloud.compatibility-verifier.enabled: false` until Spring Cloud 2026.0:

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
  config:
    import: "cosky:order-service.yaml"
cosky:
  endpoints: cosky.internal:9090
  token: ${COSKY_TOKEN}
  namespace: prod
```

**5. Stop writing Configs to 6.x, and import.**

```bash
cosky-migrate --source redis://6x-redis:6379 --target http://cosky:8080 --history
```

Exit code `0` means everything arrived, `1` that some Configs need attention, and `2` that it could not run or stopped early. Running it again continues an interrupted run, and changes nothing else.

**6. Switch.** Deploy the applications on 8.0 and stop 6.x. Then create the fixed instances from the report: nothing renews them, so nothing registers them again.

## What the tool will not do

- **Overwrite an edit.** A Config whose content on 8.0 matches no version left in 6.x was edited there, so it stays and is reported. To import it anyway, delete it on 8.0 first.
- **Touch 6.x.** It only reads, and never reads a password hash.
- **Copy secrets into the report.** It holds names, addresses and permissions, never the content of a Config or a metadata value.

For a Redis password, use `COSKY_SOURCE_URI` rather than `--source`, where `ps` cannot see it. Run `cosky-migrate --help` for everything else.

## Going back

Until you stop 6.x, going back is deploying the applications on 6.x again. Nothing writes to its keys, but Configs edited on 8.0 after the switch stay on 8.0.
</doc>

<doc title="Configuration Properties" path="guide/properties.md">
# Configuration Properties

## Server

Set these in `application.yaml`, as arguments, or as environment variables: `cosky.store.redis.uri` is `COSKY_STORE_REDIS_URI`.

### Store

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.store.type` | `redis` | `redis`, or `memory` for development: nothing survives the process |
| `cosky.store.redis.uri` | `redis://localhost:6379` | Also takes Sentinel URIs |
| `cosky.store.redis.cluster` | `false` | The URI is a seed of a Redis Cluster |
| `cosky.store.redis.tail-poll-interval` | `1s` | How often each namespace is read when no hint arrives |

### Authentication

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.auth.enabled` | `true` | Off, everyone may do everything. Only for development. |
| `cosky.auth.bootstrap-token` | `$COSKY_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN` | Becomes the `admin` ServiceAccount on the first start |
| `cosky.auth.oidc.issuer` | — | Turns OIDC on, together with `client-id` |
| `cosky.auth.oidc.client-id` | — | The Dashboard's client |
| `cosky.auth.oidc.audience` | The client | What a token must be for |
| `cosky.auth.oidc.groups-claim` | `groups` | The claim holding group names |
| `cosky.auth.oidc.scopes` | `openid, profile` | What the Dashboard asks for. Some providers send groups only when asked. |

### Watch and reads

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.watch.window` | `10000` | Events kept for resuming, and in the store's log. Should be at least the peak event rate times the longest reconnection gap. |
| `cosky.watch.window-bytes` | `64MB` | The most a replica keeps of those events in memory, per namespace. It does not limit the store's log. |
| `cosky.watch.progress-interval` | `10s` | Bookmarks sent on idle watches |
| `cosky.watch.max-per-stream` | `1000` | Watches on one stream |
| `cosky.watch.anti-entropy-interval` | `5m` | How often a replica compares its view with the store |
| `cosky.read.min-revision-timeout` | `3s` | How long a read or a resume waits for a replica to catch up |
| `cosky.view.topology-flush-interval` | `30s` | How often a replica records who watches whom. Edges expire after three times this. |

### Leases

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.lease.reaper-interval` | `1s` | How often expired leases are looked for |
| `cosky.lease.reaper-grace` | `30s` | No reaping for this long after becoming leader, or after failing to reach the store |
| `cosky.lease.reaper-max-per-tick` | `100` | Leases reaped per namespace per round |
| `cosky.lease.lock-ttl` | `15s` | How long the reaper's leadership lasts without renewal |
| `cosky.lease.protection-threshold` | `0.5` | Reaping pauses when more than this share of a namespace's leases expire at once |
| `cosky.lease.protection-min-leases` | `10` | Namespaces with fewer leases have no such pause |
| `cosky.lease.protection-max-duration` | `5m` | How long the pause lasts at most |

### From Spring

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `server.port` | `8080` | REST, Dashboard and Actuator |
| `spring.grpc.server.port` | `9090` | gRPC |
| `server.ssl.bundle`, `spring.grpc.server.ssl.bundle` | — | [TLS](./security.md#tls) |
| `spring.grpc.server.shutdown.grace-period` | `5s` | How long open streams get on shutdown |
| `management.tracing.sampling.probability` | `0.1` | Share of requests traced |
| `management.opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint` | — | Where traces go |

### Fixed limits

These cannot be set in 8.0.

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Config content | 1 MiB |
| Config history | The last 20 revisions |
| Lease TTL | 5 to 300 seconds, 30 by default |
| Instance metadata | 64 entries; keys up to 63 characters, values up to 1024 |
| Labels | 32 entries; keys up to 63 characters, values up to 253 |
| Description | 1024 characters |
| Tokens per ServiceAccount | 2 |
| One message | 2 MiB; larger results come in pages or parts |
| One page of a list | 500 by default, 1000 at most |

## Spring Boot starter

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `cosky.enabled` | `true` | Everything below |
| `cosky.endpoints` | `localhost:9090` | Servers to try in turn |
| `cosky.token` | — | Sent on every call |
| `cosky.namespace` | `default` | |
| `cosky.tls.enabled` | `false` | Connect over TLS |
| `cosky.tls.trusted-certificates` | — | A PEM file to trust, for a private CA. The JVM's trust store decides otherwise. |
| `cosky.snapshot.enabled` | `true` | Keep views on disk |
| `cosky.snapshot.dir` | `~/.cosky` | |
| `cosky.snapshot.include-config` | `true` | Snapshots are not encrypted, so false keeps Config contents off the disk |
| `cosky.registry.enabled` | `true` | Register this application |
| `cosky.registry.weight` | `1` | `0` takes no traffic |
| `cosky.registry.metadata` | — | |
| `cosky.discovery.enabled` | `true` | `DiscoveryClient` and LoadBalancer |
| `cosky.discovery.load-timeout` | `5s` | How long the first read of a service waits |
| `cosky.config.load-timeout` | `5s` | How long importing a Config waits |
| `cosky.config.refresh.enabled` | `true` | Publish `RefreshEvent` on changes |

The service name is `spring.application.name`. `spring.cloud.service-registry.auto-registration.enabled: false` also stops registering.
</doc>

<doc title="REST API" path="guide/rest-api.md">
# REST API

The management API, on port 8080. `./gradlew :api:generateOpenApi` writes the full OpenAPI 3.1 document to `api/build/openapi/cosky.yaml`, with the same schemas as gRPC, since both come from one set of protos.

## Conventions

**Authentication**: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, on everything except `GET /v1/auth/config` and [Actuator](./security.md#what-is-not-protected).

**Resources** have shared metadata and one kind-specific spec, in proto3 JSON. Empty fields are left out, and 64-bit numbers such as revisions are strings.

```json
{
  "meta": {
    "namespace": "prod",
    "name": "app.yaml",
    "revision": "42",
    "createRevision": "7",
    "updatedAt": "2026-08-18T01:00:00Z",
    "updatedBy": "serviceaccount:admin"
  },
  "config": {"format": "CONFIG_FORMAT_YAML", "content": "a: 1", "sha256": "..."}
}
```

**Names**: `{name}` is one path segment, so a `/` in a Config name is sent as `%2F`.

**Writes** replace the whole object, and read-only fields are ignored.

| Header | Means |
|---|---|
| `If-Match: "42"` | Only if it is still at revision 42 |
| `If-None-Match: *` | Only if it does not exist |

`GET` and `PUT` return the revision as `ETag`. A `PUT` of what is already there answers `{"changed": false}` and creates no revision.

**Lists** come in pages: pass `nextPageToken` as `pageToken` until it is empty. `pageSize` is 500 by default and 1000 at most, and a page can hold fewer when the objects are large. The response's `revision` and `epoch` let you start a Watch from where the list ended.

**Reading your own writes**: a replica may be slightly behind. `?minRevision=42` waits until it has reached that revision, and answers `504` after 3 seconds.

**Errors** carry a reason that does not change between versions:

```json
{
  "status": "ABORTED",
  "message": "The revision does not match.",
  "detail": {"reason": "ERROR_REASON_REVISION_CONFLICT"}
}
```

| Reason | HTTP |
|---|---|
| `RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND`, `NAMESPACE_NOT_FOUND` | 404 |
| `INVALID_ARGUMENT` | 400, with the violations in `detail` |
| `UNAUTHENTICATED` | 401 |
| `PERMISSION_DENIED` | 403 |
| `REVISION_CONFLICT`, `NAMESPACE_NOT_EMPTY` | 409 |
| `LEASE_NOT_FOUND` | 412 |
| `WATCH_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` | 429 |
| `STORE_UNAVAILABLE`, `REVISION_REGRESSION` | 503 |
| `MIN_REVISION_TIMEOUT` | 504 |

## Endpoints

### Configs

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs` | List. `?labelSelector=a=1,b=2` |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs/{name}` | |
| GET | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs/{name}/history` | Newest first. `?limit=&pageToken=` |
| POST | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs/{name}:rollback` | `{"toRevision": "41"}`. Writes that content as a new revision, and brings back a deleted Config. |
| POST | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs:import` | A zip file as the body; each entry path is a Config name |
| GET | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/configs:export` | A zip file |

### Instances

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/instances` | List. `?service=order&labelSelector=` |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/instances/{name}` | Without `meta.lease`, it stays until deleted. The service cannot change |

Leases are gRPC only: applications use the [client](./sdk.md).

### Watch

`GET /v1/namespaces/{ns}/watch?kind=KIND_CONFIG&name=&service=&fromRevision=&fromEpoch=`

Server-sent events, one proto3 JSON message per `data:` line:

| Message | Means |
|---|---|
| `snapshot` | The current state, when `fromRevision` is 0. Holds the `epoch` to resume with. |
| `events` | One revision's changes |
| `progress` | A bookmark, every 10 seconds while idle |
| `gone` | Your position is no longer valid: start over without one |
| `canceled` | The stream ends, for the reason given |

Large snapshots and revisions span several messages, marked by `more`. An `EventSource` cannot send a token: use `fetch` with a stream reader, as the Dashboard does.

### Views

Computed from the server's memory, read-only.

| Path | |
|---|---|
| `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/views/services` | Services and their instance counts |
| `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/views/topology` | Who consumes whom |
| `/v1/namespaces/{ns}/views/stats` | Counts of services, instances and Configs |

### Global objects

| Method | Path | |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/v1/namespaces` | |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/namespaces/{name}` | The smallest body is `{"namespace":{}}`. Only an empty namespace can be deleted. |
| GET | `/v1/serviceaccounts` | |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/serviceaccounts/{name}` | The smallest body is `{"serviceAccount":{}}`. `tokens` in the body is ignored. |
| POST | `/v1/serviceaccounts/{name}/tokens` | Returns the plaintext once. `{"expiresAt": "..."}` is optional. |
| DELETE | `/v1/serviceaccounts/{name}/tokens/{tokenId}` | |
| GET | `/v1/roles` | |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/roles/{name}` | |
| GET | `/v1/rolebindings` | |
| GET, PUT, DELETE | `/v1/rolebindings/{name}` | |

### Identity

| Path | |
|---|---|
| `/v1/me` | Who you are, and your effective rules |
| `/v1/auth/config` | How people sign in. Needs no token and holds public values only. |

### Operations

| Path | |
|---|---|
| `/actuator/health/liveness`, `/actuator/health/readiness` | Probes |
| `/actuator/prometheus` | [Metrics](./deployment.md#observability) |
</doc>

<doc title="Requirements" path="guide/requirements.md">
# Requirements

| Component | Version | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Server | JDK 25 | The image includes it |
| Client and starter | JDK 21 or later | |
| `cosky-migrate` | JDK 21 or later | |
| Building from source | JDK 21 and JDK 25 | Gradle does not download them |
| Spring Boot | 4.1 | For the starter |
| Spring Cloud | 2025.1 | Declares Spring Boot 4.0, so set `spring.cloud.compatibility-verifier.enabled: false` until 2026.0 |
| Redis | 7.0 or later, with `maxmemory-policy noeviction` | The server checks both at start, and refuses to run otherwise |
| Valkey | 8 | |
| Kubernetes | Anything with Kustomize | The manifests were checked with `kubectl kustomize`, and have not run on a real cluster yet |
| Browser | A current Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari | Only Chrome is tested |

Every pull request runs against Redis 7.0, Redis 7.4 and Valkey 8, on a single node and a Redis Cluster.

## Dependencies

| Library | Version |
|---|---|
| Kotlin | 2.4, compiled to Java 21. Compiling against it takes Kotlin 2.3 or later. |
| gRPC | 1.81 |
| Protobuf | 4.34 |
| Spring gRPC | 1.1 |
| Lettuce | 7.5 |

`cosky-bom` manages the versions of the CoSky modules. Spring Boot's and Spring Cloud's own BOMs manage the rest.
</doc>

<doc title="Architecture" path="guide/architecture.md">
# Architecture

This page explains how CoSky works and what it guarantees. The [design document](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/docs/architecture-redesign.md) has the reasoning behind each decision.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Apps["Applications"]
        A1["Local view<br>+ snapshot on disk"]
    end
    subgraph Server["CoSky server replicas"]
        API["gRPC and REST"] --> CACHE["Watch cache<br>per namespace"]
        REAPER["Lease reaper<br>one leader"]
    end
    REDIS[("Redis<br>objects + change log")]
    A1 -- "Put, leases" --> API
    CACHE -- "Watch" --> A1
    API -- "atomic write" --> REDIS
    REDIS -- "change log" --> CACHE
    REAPER --> REDIS
```

## The data model

Everything is a **Resource**: shared metadata and one spec. A Namespace, Config, Instance, ServiceAccount, Role and RoleBinding are all handled by one API.

A **namespace** is the unit of everything: of isolation, of ordering, and of placement, since it stays in one Redis slot. Each has its own **revision**, a counter that goes up by one with each write. An object remembers the revision that last changed it.

Global kinds live in the reserved namespace `_system`.

## A write

1. The server validates the request and checks permission.
2. One Lua script, atomically: compares the expected revision if asked, gives the namespace its next revision, stores the object, and appends the change to the namespace's log, a Redis Stream.
3. The write is acknowledged.

Writing what is already there changes nothing, and creates no revision.

## Following changes

Each replica follows each namespace's log, and keeps an immutable view of the namespace in memory, plus a window of recent changes. A write publishes a hint, so followers usually read at once. Should a hint be lost, each also polls once a second.

Watchers read those views without any lock. A slow watcher only misses intermediate views, then finds what it missed in the window. It holds back nobody else. If it falls out of the window, it gets `gone` and starts over from a snapshot of what it watches, which is the only cost.

So Redis load grows with the number of namespaces and replicas, and not with the number of clients.

Every 5 minutes, a replica also compares its view with the store. Any difference should be impossible, so it counts as a lost timeline, as below.

## What a client can rely on

- **Order**: changes within a namespace arrive in revision order, and a whole revision at once. Subscribers never see half of one.
- **Delivery**: exactly once within a stream. Across reconnections at least once, and the client drops what it already applied.
- **Resuming**: a client that reconnects to any replica continues from the revision it saw.
- **Reads** are from a local view, so they can be slightly stale. Propagation was [measured](./performance.md) at under 200 ms to 5,000 connections.
- **Writes** go to the primary, and are atomic. `minRevision` lets a REST caller read its own write from any replica.

As a safety net, a client also starts over from a fresh snapshot every 30 minutes or so.

## Leases

A process holds one lease per namespace, and attaches its instances to it, so renewing costs the same however many it has. An Instance without a lease is simply permanent, with no special handling.

One replica at a time runs the **reaper**, under a lock in Redis. It removes the instances of expired leases, with these protections, because removing live instances is worse than keeping dead ones:

1. **Grace**: after becoming leader, or failing to reach the store, it reaps nothing for 30 seconds. Clients have time to reconnect, and an expired lease can still be renewed until it is reaped.
2. **Delay**: a lease is reaped a third of its TTL after expiry. Leases cut off by one partition expire over that span, since they renew at different moments. Reaping at once would remove them one by one, and the next step would never see them together.
3. **Mass expiry**: when more than half of a namespace's leases have expired, and it has at least 10, reaping pauses and logs an error. This covers a partition between clients and servers, which the grace cannot detect. When the share falls, grace starts over. After 5 minutes, it reaps regardless.
4. **Pace**: at most 100 leases per namespace per round.

The cost is that a process that really crashed stays listed for 40 seconds by default. Callers should retry.

## When Redis loses writes

Redis replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose recent writes, and revisions then go backwards or diverge. Each namespace carries an **epoch**, a random value that changes when this is found, and a position is an epoch and a revision together.

| Detected by | Then |
|---|---|
| The log's position going backwards or missing | Every replica reloads, and every watcher gets `gone` and starts over |
| A client resuming from a revision the store does not have | That client gets `gone` |
| A lease that no longer exists | The client registers everything again |
| The periodic comparison with the store | The epoch is replaced, so all of the above follows |

The system returns to a consistent state, but what Redis lost stays lost. It takes an application to restore a Config, from its history or by writing it again.

## When servers are away

An application keeps serving its local view. On restart, it loads the [snapshot](./sdk.md#snapshots) from disk. Without a snapshot and without a server, an import that is not `optional` fails the start, so that an application does not run without its configuration.

## Why a server at all

CoSky 6.x had applications talk to Redis directly, which left the data plane without authentication, tied every client to one storage layout, and grew Redis's connections with the number of processes. Adding one small server gives authentication on every call, clients for any language, and resumable streams, while reads stay local. The server keeps nothing durable itself, so replicas can come and go.

Redis stays because it is what CoSky is for: for those who already run it, there is nothing new to operate. Those who need more durability should use a system built on consensus.
</doc>

<doc title="Performance" path="guide/performance.md">
# Performance

Measured through real gRPC and serialization, with the server in a JVM of its own on JDK 25 with compact object headers, against a Redis 7.4 container. **Load generator and server shared one 10-core laptop, over loopback**, so there was no real network, and the generator competed with the server for CPU. Treat these as an indication, and measure on your own hardware.

## Results

| Target | Result | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 50,000 instances and 10,000 Configs in a namespace | Written in 7 seconds at 64 concurrent writers. A second replica loaded them and was ready in 2 to 3.5 seconds. | Met |
| About 1 KB per instance | 86 MB for 60,000 objects, about 1.5 KB each, with the index by service and the event window | Slightly over |
| Write p99 under 20 ms | 2 ms at about 12,000 writes per second with 16 writers; 8 ms at most. Without a real network. | Met, to be measured again in one data center |
| 20,000 connections and 100,000 watches on a replica | All succeeded, in 7 seconds, and the heap grew by about 370 MB. | Met |
| Propagation p99 under 500 ms | With every write going to every connection: 89 ms to 5,000 connections, 135 ms to 10,000, and 171 to 525 ms to 20,000 in 6 runs of 7. The other run reached 5.8 seconds, and we do not know why. | **Borderline at 20,000** |
| `choose()` and reading a Config allocate nothing | `choose()` 24 to 58 million operations per second, reading a Config about 1,500 million, at about 0 bytes each | Met |

The missed propagation target is the worst case: every connection watches the same service, and the generator receives every copy on the same machine. In real traffic, an event goes only to those who depend on that service.

The connection figures come from a Linux container on the same laptop, because on macOS a client runs out of ports at about 16,000 connections. That is what stopped earlier runs at about 15,000. The load generator and the server still share 10 cores.

## The event window

A replica was killed under load, and 100 clients reconnected to another one, all watching one service. Falling out of the window means reading a fresh snapshot of that service, which costs little.

| Writes per second | Window | Clients | Deliveries per second | `gone` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| About 160 | 10,000 | 100 | About 16,000 | 0 |
| About 1,600 | 10,000 | 5 / 20 | About 8,000 / 32,000 | 0 |
| About 1,600 | 10,000 | 100 | About 160,000 | 97 to 100 |
| About 1,500 | 50,000 | 100 | About 150,000 | 0 |

So `gone` appears only when delivery cannot keep up, around 160,000 per second. The default stays at 10,000, and `cosky_watch_gone_total` after a rolling update shows whether yours should be larger.

## Large Configs

A server with 512 MB of heap, with one 1 MB Config written over and over:

| Version | Writes | Heap | Redis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Without a limit in bytes | Started failing after about 500 | Reached 510 MB | 509 MB, after 484 |
| With the default 64 MB | All 800 succeeded | Steady at about 120 MB | 825 MB, after 800 |

It restarted on that log in 4 seconds, and took 100 more writes. [Sizing](./deployment.md#sizing) covers what this means for Redis.

## Not measured

- A real network, or a real data center.
- More than one server replica under connection load.
- Redis Cluster at this scale.
- Long runs: memory over days, and leaks.

## Reproducing

```bash
COSKY_MEASURE=load COSKY_MEASURE_HEAP=4g ./gradlew :server:test --tests '*LoadMeasurement*'
```

`COSKY_LOAD_CONNECTIONS`, `COSKY_LOAD_WATCHES_PER_CONNECTION`, `COSKY_LOAD_PROPAGATION_PAUSE_MS`, `COSKY_LOAD_RATES`, `COSKY_LOAD_WINDOW` and `COSKY_LOAD_WINDOW_CLIENTS` set the shape. `COSKY_LOAD_SERVER_HEAP` sizes the server, and `COSKY_LOAD_REDIS_URI` uses a Redis you started, which a run inside a container needs. The hot paths of the client are JMH benchmarks:

```bash
./gradlew :client:jmh
```
</doc>

<doc title="Internals" path="guide/internals.md">
# Internals

For working on CoSky itself. [Architecture](./architecture.md) explains the system, the [design document](https://github.com/Ahoo-Wang/CoSky/blob/main/docs/architecture-redesign.md) the reasoning, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` how to send a change.

## Modules

| Module | Holds | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| `api` | Protos, generated code, validation, errors, the OpenAPI document | Nothing |
| `store` | The Store interface, and an implementation in memory | `api` |
| `store-redis` | The Redis Store: the only module with Lua | `store` |
| `server` | gRPC, REST, the Watch cache, the reaper, auth, views | `api`, `store`, `store-redis` |
| `client` | Connections, Watch, leases, snapshots, load balancing. No Spring and no Redis. | `api` |
| `spring-boot-starter` | ConfigData loading, refresh, discovery, registry | `client` |
| `conformance-test` | The suites the Store and the protocol must pass | `store`, `client` |
| `migration` | `cosky-migrate`. The only module that knows 6.x. | `api` |
| `examples` | A provider and a consumer, and the test that runs them | The starter |
| `dashboard` | The React frontend, with a build of its own | The REST API |
| `wiki` | This site | |

Two rules hold this together. Nothing but the server touches the Store, and clients never see Redis. And both protocols are one contract: REST is mapped from the same protos as gRPC.

## Building

```bash
./gradlew build
```

Building needs JDK 21, and the server's tests and `:server:run` need JDK 25, and Docker for the tests. Install both JDKs: Gradle does not download them. `./gradlew :server:run --args='--dev'` starts a server in memory.

The server bundles the Dashboard when `dashboard/dist` exists:

```bash
pnpm --dir dashboard install && pnpm --dir dashboard build
```

## Testing

| Level | Where | Against |
|---|---|---|
| Store conformance | `conformance-test`, run by `store` and `store-redis` | Memory, Redis, Redis Cluster |
| Protocol conformance | `conformance-test`, run by `server` | The real services over gRPC |
| Parity of the protocols | `ProtocolParityTest` | The same request over gRPC and REST ends the same way |
| Faults | `FaultInjectionTest` | A real server behind Toxiproxy: partitions, slow links, a hung store |
| Failover | `RedisStoreFailoverTest` | A real Redis losing writes |
| End to end | `examples/e2e` | The server, a provider and a consumer as separate processes |
| TLS | `TlsEndToEndTest` | Both ports, with a generated certificate |
| Dashboard | `dashboard/tests/ui` | A mock answering as the server does |
| Dashboard against the image | `dashboard/tests/ui/real-backend.spec.ts` | The page the image hosts, on that image |
| Migration | `migration` | A real Redis and a real server |

Line coverage has a floor of 90%, enforced by `./gradlew build`. New behaviour should fail a test when you take it out, so try that.

Every pull request also runs Redis 7.0 and Valkey 8, CodeQL, and an image build that starts the image and drives it.

## Lua

All of it is in `store-redis`. Each script keeps to one namespace's hash tag, and declares its keys. The layout is in the design's section on keys.

## Conventions

- Coroutines, carried by virtual threads. Reactor stays in the adapters, which Detekt enforces.
- Errors carry a stable reason, mapped to a gRPC code and an HTTP status in one place.
- A change to behaviour updates the design, and a decision gets a D-number in its table.
- Tests assert behaviour through public interfaces, against real dependencies where it matters.
</doc>
